How the ranges are worked out, what the confidence words mean and what changes them.
Where the period range comes from

Sanguine looks at the lengths of your last 12 cycles. Before you have logged a few, it starts from published averages for your age group (Bull et al. 2019) and moves towards your own pattern as cycles are added. In most life states, recent cycles and older ones count the same. A cycle that looks like a missed log, or that falls in a life change you set (such as pregnancy, or the months after stopping a hormonal method), is left out or counted less. The result is the range of days that has an 80% likelihood of holding your next period start; the calendar also shows the wider 95% range.
Confident: at least six cycles and a period range no wider than about a week.
Fair estimate: at least two cycles and a period range of up to about 11 days.
Rough estimate: fewer than two cycles, or cycles that vary so much the range is wider than about 11 days. The range is wide on purpose.
No estimate: not enough data yet, or a life change you set pauses the estimates.

Logging every period start, including the first day, matters most. Morning temperature, ovulation tests, cervical mucus and cervical position can date ovulation in a cycle after it happens, which sharpens the next period estimate and the fertile window estimate.
Logging every period start, including the first day, matters most. The more cycles you log, the narrower the range becomes.
What does not change the estimates
Symptoms, mood and notes never change an estimate. They show up in Insights so you can see your own patterns, but there is no published evidence that they predict when a period starts.
How well it has done for you
When a cycle ends, Sanguine checks whether the range it gave at the start of that cycle held the real start date. Insights, Your accuracy, shows the count.

Estrogen and progesterone are at their lowest, and bleeding carries iron out of the body. In a study that tracked 397 substances in the blood and urine of 34 women across the cycle, amino acids and vitamin D were higher during the period than in the second half of the cycle.
Any movement that feels good, such as a walk, a swim, yoga or your usual training, can lift your mood and energy. Rest is fine too.
Reviews of more than 1,000 trials find that exercise improves mood and energy, and a single session lifts mood on average. In smaller trials, regular exercise also eased period pain.

NHMRC Nutrient Reference Values: iron. Singh and others 2023, British Journal of Sports Medicine. Weinstein and others 2024, Psychosomatic Medicine. Armour and others 2019, Cochrane review of exercise for period pain. Daily and others 2015, Pain Medicine (ginger). 2024 reviews of ginger and of omega-3 for period pain. Hsu and others 2024, Nutrients (zinc). Draper and others 2018, Scientific Reports.
After the period, estrogen rises as a follicle grows in the ovary. In the same study, amino acids and fats in the blood were higher in this phase than in the second half of the cycle.
Exercise lifts mood and energy. If you feel energetic, this can be a good time to try harder sessions.
Reviews of more than 1,000 trials find that exercise improves mood and energy. Performance itself differs little between phases, so let how you feel decide how hard to go.

Singh and others 2023, British Journal of Sports Medicine. Wender and others 2022, Frontiers in Psychology. McNulty and others 2020, Sports Medicine. Draper and others 2018, Scientific Reports.
Estrogen peaks and a surge of luteinising hormone triggers ovulation. In the same study, vitamin D and a marker of vitamin B6 were lower around ovulation than during the period.
Train as usual, and warm up well before sports with jumping, landing and quick changes of direction.
Knee ligaments loosen slightly around this time in some studies, but reviews find no phase with clearly more knee injuries. Warm-up programmes halve knee ligament injuries at any time of the cycle.

Draper and others 2018, Scientific Reports. Gaskins and others 2009, American Journal of Clinical Nutrition (fibre). Systematic review of cycle phase and knee injury measures, 2022. Webster and Hewett 2018, Journal of Orthopaedic Research.

Progesterone rises and body temperature goes up by a few tenths of a degree. In the same study, 39 amino acids and 18 fats in the blood were lower in this phase, and so was serotonin, a messenger linked to mood. The authors suggest the body is using the amino acids and fats to build tissue, including the lining of the uterus.
Keep moving: exercise lifts mood and energy. In warm weather, drink regularly and give yourself more time to cool down.

Reviews of more than 1,000 trials find that exercise improves mood, and a single session lifts it on average. Progesterone raises core temperature and the temperature at which sweating starts by about half a degree.

Draper and others 2018, Scientific Reports. Kriengsinyos and others 2004, American Journal of Physiology. NHMRC Nutrient Reference Values (magnesium, B12). Tucker and others 2024, Nutrition Reviews. Benton and others 2020, PLoS ONE. Singh and others 2023, British Journal of Sports Medicine. Weinstein and others 2024, Psychosomatic Medicine. Gatorade Sports Science Institute review of hydration in active women.
Progesterone and estrogen fall in the days before the period. Many women notice lower mood, bloating, cravings or lighter sleep in these days.
When your mood or energy is low, a walk, a bike ride, a swim, yoga or a dance class can lift it. A regular wind-down before bed can help with sleep.

Reviews of more than 1,000 trials find that exercise improves mood, and walking, yoga and strength training do especially well. In a review of 15 trials, women who exercised also reported fewer premenstrual symptoms.

Singh and others 2023, British Journal of Sports Medicine. Noetel and others 2024, BMJ. Pearce and others 2020, BJGP Open. Regular activity on most days, with muscle-strengthening at least twice a week. On low days, even a short walk helps.
This is Australia's physical activity guideline. Reviews of more than 1,000 trials find that exercise improves mood and energy.

Australian Dietary Guidelines 2013. NHMRC Nutrient Reference Values. Australia's Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour Guidelines. Singh and others 2023, British Journal of Sports Medicine. Wender and others 2022, Frontiers in Psychology.

Iron-rich foods, such as red meat, chicken, fish, lentils, tofu or leafy greens, with vitamin C from citrus, capsicum or tomato in the same meal. For example: a beef and broccoli stir-fry, lentil dahl with a squeeze of lemon, or a spinach and chickpea curry with tomatoes.
Monthly bleeding is why women aged 19 to 50 need 18 mg of iron a day, against 8 mg for men. Vitamin C in the same meal helps the body absorb iron from plant foods.
Omega-3 fats from oily fish such as salmon, sardines or mackerel, or from walnuts, chia and linseed. For example: sardines on wholegrain toast, or salmon with greens and rice.
Omega-3 is the fat tested in the period-pain trials, taken as a supplement (see below). Whether eating it as food eases pain is untested; fish twice a week fits general heart-health advice.
Vitamin C from kiwifruit, oranges, strawberries, capsicum or broccoli, alongside iron-rich meals. For example: muesli with kiwifruit and yoghurt, or a chicken and capsicum stir-fry.
Vitamin C helps the body absorb iron from plant foods, which helps refill what the period used. No study shows a special need for it in this phase.

Foods rich in B vitamins, especially riboflavin and thiamine, such as milk, yoghurt, eggs, wholegrain cereals, legumes, mushrooms and leafy greens. For example: porridge made with milk, or eggs and mushrooms on wholegrain toast.

In a 10-year study of more than 3,000 nurses, women who got the most riboflavin (B2) and thiamine (B1) from food were 25 to 35% less likely to develop premenstrual symptoms. B vitamins from tablets showed no such link, the study only observed, and nobody has tested whether timing in the cycle matters.
Zinc from beef, chicken, oysters, pumpkin seeds, chickpeas or cashews. For example: a chicken and chickpea salad topped with pumpkin seeds, or a beef burrito bowl.
Zinc helps cells grow and repair, and women need 8 mg a day. In 6 small trials, zinc supplements eased period pain. Nobody has tested whether eating more zinc at this time of the cycle helps.
Fibre-rich foods such as oats, legumes, vegetables, wholegrains and fruit with the skin on. For example: overnight oats with berries, or a bean and vegetable soup.

Fibre helps the body clear estrogen through the gut, which is the idea behind eating more of it around the estrogen peak. But in a study of 250 women, those who ate the most fibre had lower hormone levels and more cycles without ovulation, so more is not always better. Fibre's everyday benefits for the gut are well established.
Foods with vitamin D and vitamin B6, such as oily fish, eggs, chickpeas, potatoes and bananas. For example: a salmon and potato traybake, or a chickpea curry followed by a banana.
One small study found lower vitamin D and vitamin B6 markers around ovulation. Nobody has yet tested whether eating more of them at this time helps.

A source of protein at each meal, such as eggs, Greek yoghurt, fish, meat, tofu or legumes. For example: eggs on toast, Greek yoghurt with nuts, or a lentil and feta salad. Feeling hungrier in this phase is common.

Amino acids, the building blocks of protein, were lower in this phase, and a small study found a higher need for one of them. On average women eat a little more now, in step with a small rise in the energy the body uses at rest.
Magnesium from leafy greens, nuts, seeds, legumes, wholegrains and dark chocolate. For example: a handful of almonds, brown rice with black beans, or a spinach and pumpkin-seed salad.
Women need 310 to 320 mg a day. Small trials of magnesium supplements reported fewer premenstrual symptoms, but studies of magnesium from food are mixed.

Vitamin B12 from meat, fish, eggs and dairy, or from fortified plant milks and nutritional yeast if you eat a plant-based diet. For example: a tuna sandwich, or a smoothie made with fortified soy milk.
B12 is needed to make red blood cells, and running low causes tiredness. No study links B12 needs to this phase; it is here because it is easy to miss without animal foods.

Calcium-rich foods such as milk, yoghurt, cheese, calcium-fortified soy drinks, tofu set with calcium or canned salmon with the bones. For example: yoghurt with fruit, a cheese and salad sandwich, or a tofu stir-fry.

In a 10-year study of more than 3,000 nurses, women who got the most calcium from food were about 40% less likely to develop premenstrual symptoms, and in a trial of 466 women calcium eased them more than a placebo did. Calcium also supports bone health at every age.

Regular meals with slow-digesting carbohydrate, such as oats, brown rice, wholegrain bread, sweet potato or legumes. For example: a sweet potato and black bean bowl, or wholegrain toast with peanut butter.
Cravings for carbohydrate are common before a period. Regular wholegrain meals are a common suggestion for steadier energy and mood, but few trials have tested it.
Zinc: in 6 small trials with 739 women, zinc supplements eased period pain.
A 2024 review pooled the trials. Doses varied widely; one trial gave 40 mg of zinc sulfate a day to 103 high-school students. More than 40 mg a day over a long time can lower copper levels.
Ginger: in small trials, ginger powder taken in the first 3 to 4 days of the period eased period pain.

A 2024 review of 24 studies found less pain than with a placebo and no clear difference from anti-inflammatory pain relievers. Trials used 750 to 2,000 mg of ginger powder a day. The trials were small and their results varied.
Omega-3 (fish oil): taken daily for 2 to 3 months, it eased period pain in small trials.
A 2024 review of 12 studies with 881 women found less period pain with 300 to 1,800 mg of omega-3 a day. Reviews disagree on how large the effect is.
Calcium: in one large trial, a daily calcium supplement eased premenstrual symptoms. Calcium-rich foods count towards the same amount.

The trial gave 1,200 mg of calcium a day for three cycles to 466 women. Symptom scores fell more than with a placebo, though the placebo group also improved, and a maker of calcium products helped fund it.
Vitamin B6: small trials for premenstrual symptoms show mixed results. B6 can damage nerves, sometimes at under 50 mg a day: stop and see a doctor if you feel tingling, burning or numbness.

A review of 9 trials found some benefit, but the trials were of poor quality. Since 2023 the TGA has required a nerve warning on products with more than 10 mg a day. Several products can contain B6, also listed as pyridoxine, so check every label.
Magnesium: a few small, older trials reported fewer premenstrual symptoms; reviews call the evidence limited.
The trials had 28 to 38 women each, and another study found no benefit. Studies comparing blood magnesium in women with and without premenstrual symptoms are inconclusive.
